families.s: HSE warehousing, storage-racking and load-stability guidance
families.t: racking design, pallets, load limits, aisles, inspection, damage, access, stacking, lift trucks and supervision
f: Warehousing risk management covers storage, manual handling, mechanical handling, site transport and work at height.
Storage racking should be designed, installed and used for the loads and pallets it carries.
Load limits and configuration restrictions should be known and followed.
Aisles should provide adequate clearance for the largest lift trucks and loads using them.
Racking damage should be reported, assessed and repaired or isolated before continued use.
Stacked steel, metal stock and other materials require stable systems that prevent collapse or uncontrolled movement.
Storage racking should not be used as an improvised means of access.
Warehousing and storage operations should be supervised by people competent in the applicable risks.
families.g: Racking risk depends on design, installation, pallet and load, impact damage, aisle clearance, stacking, lift-truck operation, inspection, repairs and unauthorised access.

families.s: HSE rider-operated lift-truck training, safe-use and examination guidance
families.t: selection, operator training, supervision, pedestrians, loads, stability, maintenance, daily checks and thorough examination
f: Lift trucks are involved in a substantial proportion of workplace-transport accidents.
Operators should complete appropriate basic training before being allowed to operate relevant lift trucks.
Training should be followed by specific job and site familiarisation.
Pedestrians should be protected through layout, separation, traffic rules and supervision.
Loads should remain stable, secure and within the truck's rated capacity.
Seat restraints and other operator protection should be used where fitted and required.
Pre-use checks, planned maintenance and defect reporting are required.
Lift trucks require thorough examination at the applicable interval or under a competent-person scheme.
families.g: Lift-truck risk depends on truck type, load, route, pedestrians, visibility, speed, surface, operator competence, restraint, maintenance and examination.

families.s: HSE loading-bay, dock-leveller and vehicle-tail-lift guidance
families.t: traffic exclusion, level ground, trailer restraint, dock gaps, falls, trapping, roll cages, guards and communication
f: Loading and unloading areas should be separated from unrelated traffic and pedestrians.
Vehicles and trailers should be positioned on firm level ground and prevented from moving unexpectedly.
Dock levellers bridge variable height differences and require guarding where trapping or shearing is possible.
Loading-bay gaps can cause lift trucks to fall if a vehicle departs unexpectedly.
Vehicle restraint, key control or other systems can prevent premature drive-away.
Tail lifts can trap hands and feet during raising and lowering.
Roll cages and loads should be controlled so they cannot fall from a raised tail lift.
Vehicle tail lifts are lifting equipment and require suitable planning, maintenance and examination.
families.g: Loading-bay risk depends on vehicle movement, dock gap, trailer support, dock leveller, tail lift, roll cages, pedestrians, communication, lighting and maintenance.

families.s: HSE workplace reversing, parking and pedestrian-route guidance
families.t: elimination, one-way routes, marked zones, banksmen, visibility, barriers, refuges, driver induction and pedestrian separation
f: Reversing contributes to a significant share of fatal workplace-transport incidents.
The need to reverse should be eliminated where possible using one-way or drive-through layouts.
Where reversing is unavoidable, designated areas should be planned and kept clear of pedestrians.
A trained signaller may be used where other controls do not provide adequate visibility and separation.
Visiting drivers should be told the site layout and rules.
Parking areas should separate pedestrians and vehicles using routes, exclusion zones, barriers or bollards.
Loading bays need pedestrian exits or refuges so people are not trapped by vehicles.
Road markings, lighting, mirrors, cameras and alarms may support but do not replace safe layout and segregation.
families.g: Reversing risk depends on layout, visibility, vehicle size, pedestrian routes, driver familiarity, banksman control, lighting, barriers, parking and traffic volume.

families.s: HSE excavation, trench, underground-service and temporary-support guidance
families.t: collapse, support, underground services, spoil, water, access, inspection, adjacent structures and plant exclusion
f: Before excavation starts, the need for temporary support should be determined and planned.
Excavation work should not begin until underground services have been identified and controlled.
Trench and excavation sides may require shoring, shielding, battering or another engineered solution.
Spoil, materials and plant should be kept far enough from the edge to avoid overloading and falling material.
Safe access and egress should be provided.
Water ingress and pumping can affect excavation stability and require assessment.
Adjacent foundations and structures may require surveys and engineering advice.
Excavations and supports should be inspected by a competent person after events that could affect stability.
families.g: Excavation risk depends on soil, depth, water, support design, services, edge loads, adjacent structures, access, plant movement, inspection and weather.

families.s: HSE demolition, structural-stability and temporary-works management guidance
families.t: competent planning, structural information, sequencing, temporary support, exclusion, written arrangements, design checks and change control
f: Demolition is construction work and must be planned and managed under the applicable construction duties.
Alteration, demolition and dismantling should be planned and carried out by competent people to avoid unplanned collapse.
Clients should provide available structural information and significant design assumptions.
The contractor should use that information to develop a safe method and sequence.
Temporary supports, facade retention, falsework and shoring require competent design and installation.
Workers and passers-by should be protected from collapse and debris using exclusion and containment measures.
Key demolition, dismantling or structural-alteration arrangements should be recorded in writing before work starts.
Temporary works require coordination, design checks, inspection and controlled modification comparable to permanent works.
families.g: Demolition and temporary-works risk depends on structural form and condition, sequence, temporary support, design checks, adjacent buildings, debris, exclusion, competence and change control.
